docs.text: Beneath the Mesa Assessing Aquifer, Well, and Acequia Water Resources Across Sandoval County, New Mexico ENG 220 · Team 23 Open the live app · View the code on GitHub About the project Water scarcity is a persistent challenge across New Mexico. Sandoval County spans several hydrogeologic settings, and its communities depend on a mix of groundwater wells, surface water, and acequia irrigation systems. This project evaluates the condition and long-term viability of those water resources across the county, with Cuba, New Mexico, on the eastern edge of the San Juan Basin, as a focused case study. The project is motivated by concern about declining groundwater near Cuba, but rather than assume how severe that decline is or what is causing it, we test what the available public data actually show. Approach The study works at two levels: County-wide screening. Map and compare aquifers, wells, water levels, water quality, and acequia and surface-water features across Sandoval County. Because the county crosses several geologic regions, comparisons are grouped by region or aquifer system instead of treating the county as one uniform aquifer. Cuba case study. A closer look at the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation near Cuba, using San Juan Basin aquifer datasets alongside nearby well, water-level, and water-quality records. The analysis focuses on measurable indicators such as depth to water, water-level change over time, well depth, aquifer unit, and salinity, rather than a full hydrologic model. Where records are sparse, the results say so instead of filling the gaps. Research questions How do groundwater levels vary across Sandoval County, and which areas show sustained decline, stability, or recovery? What do well records show about well depth, depth to water, and the aquifer units that communities rely on? Do the available data support the concern that Cuba's main groundwater source is approaching severe depletion? How do the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation compare near Cuba in extent, thickness, hydraulic properties, water levels, and water quality? How does groundwater quality, including salinity, vary across the county and near Cuba? Where are acequias located, what surface water do they depend on, and which communities do they serve? Do changes in groundwater levels line up with nearby surface-water or acequia conditions, or are the records too limited to tell? Where is monitoring coverage strong, and where are the most important data gaps? Which indicators can be combined into a dashboard that shows water-resource stress without overstating how certain the data are? How this site is organized The site follows the project's stages, from collecting data to presenting results. Each stage page explains what was done, which files it produced, and who led it. Page What it covers 1. Data collection The datasets we use, where they come from, and why we chose them 2. Data cleaning How the raw data is filtered and prepared for analysis 3. Analysis and visualizations The methods and charts used to answer each research question 4. Streamlit app What the interactive dashboard shows and how to run it 5. Final report The written report and the project proposal 6. Presentation and video The presentation slides and the seven-minute team video Findings What the data show, and where they are too limited to say Timeline What was completed at each course checkpoint Team Who did what

docs.text: 2. Data cleaning Lead: James Wauneka This stage turns the raw downloads into tables the analysis code can use directly. Cleaning makes the data correct and consistent; it doesn't draw conclusions. Averaging, trends, and narrowing to the Cuba area happen in the analysis stage. Cleaned files Cleaned file Rows Made from What it holds groundwater_levels_monthly.csv 2,673 USGS statistics ( dataset 1 ) Monthly mean depth to water for 9 wells, June 1998 to September 2026 aquifer_tests.csv 179 NM Office of the State Engineer aquifer tests One row per aquifer test in Sandoval County, 1930 to 2008, with formation, well construction, and hydraulic properties James's MATLAB script, cleaning/clean_csvs.m , makes both files. Both follow the conventions below. The groundwater file was checked against the raw data: it has the same rows, dates, and values, with no duplicates. Columns groundwater_levels_monthly.csv : site_id , site_name , latitude , longitude , date , source , depth_to_water_ft aquifer_tests.csv : site_id , site_name , latitude , longitude , date , source , formation , well_depth_ft , screen_top_ft , screen_bottom_ft , depth_to_water_ft , pumping_rate_gpm , transmissivity_drawdown_ft2_per_day , transmissivity_recovery_ft2_per_day , storativity , specific_capacity_gpm_per_ft , hydraulic_conductivity_ft_per_day In both files, depth_to_water_ft is depth below land surface, so a larger number means a lower water table. Wells in the groundwater file site_id Site name Months First Last USGS-351357106323001 12N.04E.29.433 SANDIA SITE 323 1999-02 2026-04 USGS-351357106323002 12N.04E.29.433A SANDIA SITE 328 1999-01 2026-04 USGS-351357106323003 12N.04E.29.433B SANDIA SITE 198 1999-01 2015-09 USGS-351515106410401 12N.02E.24.144 LINCOLN MIDDLE SCHOOL 325 1998-06 2026-09 USGS-351515106410402 12N.02E.24.144A LINCOLN MIDDLE SCHOOL 310 1998-06 2026-09 USGS-351515106410403 12N.02E.24.144B LINCOLN MIDDLE SCHOOL 317 1998-06 2026-09 USGS-351821106333901 13N.04E.31.343 BERNALILLO SITE 306 1999-09 2026-08 USGS-351821106333902 13N.04E.31.343A BERNALILLO SITE PIEZ 2 238 1999-09 2021-02 USGS-354056106215801 17N.05E.24.344 DOME ROAD WELL 328 1999-02 2026-06 Wells with an A or B suffix are at the same location as the well without one but are measured at different depths, so they stay separate. Running the script In MATLAB, set the current folder to the repository's root folder (the one that contains data/ ), then run one of these: clean_csvs % make both cleaned files clean_csvs('groundwater') % groundwater levels only clean_csvs('aquifer') % aquifer tests only The script reads data/water_flow_data_sandoval_county_sources.csv (an identical copy of dataset 1) and data/ose_aquifer_test_wells.csv , and writes to data/clean/ . As it runs, it prints checks such as row counts, duplicate rows, and the list of formation names, so problems are easy to spot. Where files go What Where Example Raw downloads (never edited) data/ data/ose_aquifer_test_wells.csv Cleaning scripts cleaning/ cleaning/clean_csvs.m Cleaned files data/clean/ data/clean/aquifer_tests.csv Every cleaned file is made by a script in cleaning/ that reads the raw file and writes the cleaned one, so anyone can rerun it and get the same result. Python or MATLAB both work. If a step is done by hand in Excel, write it down under How each file was cleaned . How each file was cleaned Groundwater levels Reads every column as text and standardizes the column names. Keeps groundwater-level rows ( parameter_code 72019) that are monthly means ( interval_type is month and parent_statistic_name is Mean ). That leaves 2,673 rows. Renames columns to the shared names: monitoring_location_id → site_id , monitoring_location_name → site_name , y → latitude , x → longitude , start_date → date , and arithmetic_mean → depth_to_water_ft . Sets source to USGS . Keeps wells with an A or B suffix as separate sites. Checks for duplicate site-and-date rows (there are none) and counts the wells (9). Sorts by site and date, and writes the file with blank cells for missing values. Aquifer tests Reads every column as text and standardizes the column names. This also removes the hidden byte-order mark from the first column name. Keeps Sandoval County rows ( COUNTY NAME is SANDOVAL ): 179 tests. Every test is kept, even when a well has more than one. Keeps the 16 columns the analysis needs, renamed as listed under Columns . Empty and administrative columns are left out, such as ground surface elevation (blank for every Sandoval row), GlobalID , and Entered By . Converts numbers stored as text, removes commas, and leaves placeholders such as NA and -9999 blank. Converts dates such as 11/12/2002 12:00:00 AM to 2002-11-12 . Cleans formation names: trims extra spaces, converts them to uppercase, and fixes the misspelling SAANDSTONE . Sets source to NM OSE and puts the shared columns first. Checks for columns that are empty or identical in every row (none were), then sorts by site and date and writes the file. Conventions for cleaned files Every cleaned file follows the same rules, so the files can be combined and charted the same way. File names: lowercase with underscores, describing what's inside, such as groundwater_levels_monthly.csv . No dates, versions, or "final" in names; GitHub keeps the history. Column names: lowercase with underscores, with the unit at the end, such as well_depth_ft or transmissivity_drawdown_ft2_per_day . Shared columns: every file starts with these, using the same names: Column Contents site_id The source's ID for the well or site, as text site_name The well or site name latitude , longitude Decimal degrees date YYYY-MM-DD source Where the data came from, such as USGS or NM OSE Rows: one row per measurement, sorted by site_id and then date . Values: Numbers only, with no units, commas, or ranges inside cells. Missing values left blank. Never use 0 , N/A , or -9999 , which charts would plot as real values. Dates as YYYY-MM-DD . Text trimmed of extra spaces and spelled consistently. File format: comma-separated, UTF-8, one header row, and no index column. In pandas, use df.to_csv(path, index=False) . From Excel, save as "CSV UTF-8". What to keep: IDs, location, date, and every measurement the analysis might use. Drop columns that are empty or identical in every row. Problems and decisions Problem Decision One hydraulic conductivity value is a range, 11 to 21 (Centex American Gypsum Company well) Uses the midpoint, 16 ft/day 104 tests have 1/1/1900 as the start water-level date, meaning the date is unknown Treated as unknown. The date column isn't in the cleaned file. 30 tests are dated January 1, which may mean only the year is known Kept as is Formation misspelled as POINT LOOKOUT SAANDSTONE Fixed to POINT LOOKOUT SANDSTONE Many tests are missing measurements, such as formation (blank for 54 of 179 tests) and storativity (blank for 165) Left blank, as the conventions require Still open Incomplete well IDs in the aquifer-test file. In the raw file, 157 of the 179 OSE POD ID values are incomplete, and 85 are just RG-- . As a result, site_id groups unrelated wells together: the cleaned file has 73 site IDs but about 149 distinct wells by name and location. Until this is fixed, the analysis should tell wells apart by site_name , latitude , and longitude , not by site_id . One formation name is still misspelled. AGUA ZARCA SANDSTONE MEMBER OF SIERRA NACIEMIENTO should be NACIMIENTO . It can be added to the list of fixes in the script's clean_formation function. Still to clean These raw files aren't cleaned yet. See Data collection for what each one contains. NM Bureau of Geology groundwater levels (dataset 2): convert UTM easting and northing to latitude and longitude, after checking the zone and datum. Rio Puerco at Cuba (dataset 4): the streamflow and gage-height measurements. Wells with well logs (dataset 7): convert UTM coordinates to latitude and longitude, and trim the extra spaces in well IDs. Other USGS measurements in dataset 1: streamflow, reservoir storage, and water quality, one cleaned file per measurement, following the groundwater-levels pattern. Datasets 3, 5, and 6 don't need cleaning: dataset 3 has no locations until its map layer is downloaded, and datasets 5 and 6 are publications rather than data tables.

docs.text: 1. Data collection Lead: Dylan Gonzales This stage covers finding public datasets that can answer the research questions , downloading them, and recording where each one comes from. For each dataset, Dylan wrote a one-page brief. It covers what the dataset contains, which research questions it can help answer, which plots to make, and what the data can't show. A one-page guide compares all seven: Data plotting guide for datasets 1–7 (PDF) What the data can and can't show Together, the datasets are strongest for groundwater trends at monitored wells (Q1), well characteristics (Q2), comparing the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation (Q4), stream observations at Cuba (Q7), monitoring coverage and gaps (Q8), and dashboard indicators (Q9). None of them shows on its own whether Cuba's municipal aquifer is being depleted, or which formation Cuba's wells draw from. Every chart and caption should say whether it describes Cuba itself, Sandoval County, or the wider San Juan Basin. Datasets # Dataset From Relevance to Cuba Best for Brief 1 Groundwater-level statistics USGS Countywide; no Cuba wells Q1, Q8, Q9 PDF 2 Groundwater levels NM Bureau of Geology Countywide; nearest well about 24 miles from Cuba Q2, Q8, Q1 PDF 3 Aquifer sensitivity NM Water Data Not established; the file has no locations Q9, once checked PDF 4 Rio Puerco at Cuba USGS At Cuba (river, not groundwater) Q7, Q8, Q9 PDF 5 Ojo Alamo Sandstone USGS map plate Regional geology Q4, Q2 PDF 6 San Jose Formation near Lindrith NM Geological Society Regional geology Q4, Q2 PDF 7 Wells with well logs NM Office of the State Engineer 6 Sandoval well logs; Cuba link not verified Q2, Q8 PDF The raw files are in the repository's data/ folder , and Word versions of the briefs are in docs/files/ . 1. USGS groundwater-level statistics File: data1_water_flow_data_sandoval_county_sources.csv Source: USGS Water Data statistics download USGS monthly and yearly statistics for 30 monitoring sites in Sandoval County (9 wells, 17 stream gages, 2 canals, and 2 reservoirs), with records from 1926 to 2026. Besides depth to groundwater, it covers streamflow, reservoir storage, suspended sediment, water temperature, and water quality (specific conductance, dissolved oxygen, pH, and turbidity). Dylan's brief covers the groundwater part: 9,462 records from 9 wells at four sites (Sandia, Lincoln Middle School, Bernalillo, and Dome Road), from about 1998 to 2026. Use for: depth-to-water trends at each well, a map of the wells, and a timeline of monitoring coverage. Cautions: none of the wells are in Cuba. Monthly, calendar-year, and water-year rows summarize the same measurements, so use one type at a time. A larger depth to water means a lower water table. 2. NM Bureau of Geology groundwater levels File: data2_groundwater_sandoval_county.csv Source: New Mexico Water Data: groundwater levels 456 depth-to-water measurements from 87 wells in Sandoval County, 1997 to 2019, from the New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources. Each record has the well's location (UTM easting and northing), well depth, hole depth, measurement date, and depth to water below ground. Use for: a map of the wells, well depth compared with depth to water, time series for wells measured more than once, and measurement counts per well. Cautions: the nearest well is about 24 miles from Cuba. Many wells were measured only once, which can't show a trend. Check the UTM zone and datum before mapping. 3. Aquifer sensitivity File: data3_Aquifer_Sensitivity.csv Source: New Mexico Water Data: aquifer sensitivity ( map layer ) 613 mapped areas, each with a sensitivity class (339 Moderate, 152 High, and 122 Less) and the area's size and perimeter. The CSV has no coordinates or shapes, so it can't be mapped or matched to Cuba on its own. Use for: a sensitivity indicator on the dashboard (Q9), once the map layer is downloaded and it's clear what "sensitivity" measures. Cautions: the class counts are numbers of mapped areas, not shares of land. The file doesn't state the units for area and perimeter. 4. Rio Puerco at Cuba Files: data4_monitoring-location-metadata.csv , data4_field-measurements.csv , data4_channel-measurements.csv Source: USGS station 08332525 on the Water Quality Portal The only dataset measured at Cuba itself: USGS station 08332525 on the Rio Puerco. The three files hold the station's details and coordinates, 4 gage-height readings (2019 to 2024), and 10 streamflow measurements (2019 to 2026). Six of the streamflow visits found no flow, and the other four measured 6.89 to 20.40 cubic feet per second. Use for: a scatter plot of flow by date, a count of zero-flow and flowing visits, and a map of the station relative to Cuba. Cautions: these are occasional visits, not a continuous record, so zero-flow readings don't mean the river is dry all year. The station measures the river, not Cuba's groundwater or water supply. 5. Ojo Alamo Sandstone File: data5_ojo_alamo_sandstone_pub.pdf Source: USGS, Hydrogeology of the Ojo Alamo Sandstone in the San Juan Structural Basin (Hydrologic Atlas 720-B) A USGS map plate (1990) of the Ojo Alamo Sandstone across the San Juan Basin, showing depth to the top of the sandstone, its thickness, and wells completed in it. Use for: an annotated map, or a side-by-side comparison with the San Jose Formation (Q4). Cautions: this is a historical regional map, not current conditions, and it isn't a table to plot. It doesn't show that Cuba's wells draw from this formation. 6. San Jose Formation near Lindrith File: data6_cuba_mesa_member_of_san_jose_formation.pdf Source: Blandford et al. (2025), " San Jose Formation Hydrostratigraphy and Groundwater Conditions in the Vicinity of Lindrith, New Mexico ," New Mexico Geological Society Guidebook 75, pp. 235–246, doi:10.56577/FFC-75.235 A study of about 840 km² near Lindrith that uses more than 350 geophysical logs and 85 well-drilling logs. It identifies four water-bearing units in the San Jose Formation, maps the thickness of the Cuba Mesa Member, and maps groundwater levels. Use for: comparing with the Ojo Alamo Sandstone (Q4), and explaining which units wells reach (Q2). Cautions: the study is centered near Lindrith, not on Cuba's wells. The Cuba Mesa Member is a candidate water-bearing unit around Cuba, but the paper doesn't show that Cuba pumps from it. 7. Wells with well logs File: data7_Wells With Well Log Information.csv Source: NM Office of the State Engineer, Water Rights Reporting System, "Wells With Well Log Information" report for the San Juan basin Drilling records for 6 wells in Sandoval County, drilled between 1978 and 2022, with location, borehole depth, depth where water was first found, and driller. They come from a San Juan basin download of 1,379 well logs across four counties, which Dylan's brief describes. Use for: comparing borehole depth with first-water depth (Q2), and mapping where well logs exist (Q8). Cautions: first-water depth was recorded on drilling day, not as a current water level. The file doesn't identify Cuba's municipal wells or the formation each well draws from. Other raw data in the repository ose_aquifer_test_wells.csv : New Mexico Office of the State Engineer aquifer-test records, 3,455 statewide and 179 in Sandoval County, including well depth, screened interval, geologic formation, and hydraulic properties such as transmissivity and storativity. It's cleaned into data/clean/aquifer_tests.csv (see Data cleaning ). Source: To be added: link to the page this file was downloaded from. water_flow_data_sandoval_county_sources.csv : an identical copy of dataset 1. The cleaning script reads this copy. Still to collect Cuba's municipal well records: well IDs, the formation each well draws from, pumping volumes, and water-level history, from the Village of Cuba or the NM Office of the State Engineer. Every brief points to these records as the missing piece for answering whether Cuba's aquifer is being depleted (Q3). Aquifer sensitivity map layer: the map layer for dataset 3 and documentation of what its classes mean, to check whether it covers Cuba. Digital aquifer data near Cuba: USGS San Juan Basin digital aquifer data for the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation, to go beyond the maps in datasets 5 and 6. Water quality and salinity: the NM Bureau of Geology San Juan Basin Brackish Water Assessment and New Mexico Water Data records. Acequias: locations and service areas of acequias and community ditches from the NM Interstate Stream Commission. More water-level records: National Ground-Water Monitoring Network and Healy Collaborative Groundwater Monitoring Network data. Shallow groundwater depth: the mean annual depth to groundwater for the shallow riparian aquifer dataset. County boundary: a Sandoval County boundary layer to organize the maps. docs.text: Lead: Dylan Gonzales This stage covers finding public datasets that can answer the research questions , downloading them, and recording where each one comes from. For each dataset, Dylan wrote a one-page brief. It covers what the dataset contains, which research questions it can help answer, which plots to make, and what the data can't show. A one-page guide compares all seven: Data plotting guide for datasets 1–7 (PDF)
docs.title: 1. Data collection

docs.text: Together, the datasets are strongest for groundwater trends at monitored wells (Q1), well characteristics (Q2), comparing the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation (Q4), stream observations at Cuba (Q7), monitoring coverage and gaps (Q8), and dashboard indicators (Q9). None of them shows on its own whether Cuba's municipal aquifer is being depleted, or which formation Cuba's wells draw from. Every chart and caption should say whether it describes Cuba itself, Sandoval County, or the wider San Juan Basin.
docs.title: What the data can and can't show

docs.title: Datasets

docs.text: File: data1_water_flow_data_sandoval_county_sources.csv Source: USGS Water Data statistics download USGS monthly and yearly statistics for 30 monitoring sites in Sandoval County (9 wells, 17 stream gages, 2 canals, and 2 reservoirs), with records from 1926 to 2026. Besides depth to groundwater, it covers streamflow, reservoir storage, suspended sediment, water temperature, and water quality (specific conductance, dissolved oxygen, pH, and turbidity). Dylan's brief covers the groundwater part: 9,462 records from 9 wells at four sites (Sandia, Lincoln Middle School, Bernalillo, and Dome Road), from about 1998 to 2026. Use for: depth-to-water trends at each well, a map of the wells, and a timeline of monitoring coverage. Cautions: none of the wells are in Cuba. Monthly, calendar-year, and water-year rows summarize the same measurements, so use one type at a time. A larger depth to water means a lower water table.
docs.title: 1. USGS groundwater-level statistics

docs.text: File: data2_groundwater_sandoval_county.csv Source: New Mexico Water Data: groundwater levels 456 depth-to-water measurements from 87 wells in Sandoval County, 1997 to 2019, from the New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources. Each record has the well's location (UTM easting and northing), well depth, hole depth, measurement date, and depth to water below ground. Use for: a map of the wells, well depth compared with depth to water, time series for wells measured more than once, and measurement counts per well. Cautions: the nearest well is about 24 miles from Cuba. Many wells were measured only once, which can't show a trend. Check the UTM zone and datum before mapping.
docs.title: 2. NM Bureau of Geology groundwater levels

docs.text: File: data3_Aquifer_Sensitivity.csv Source: New Mexico Water Data: aquifer sensitivity ( map layer ) 613 mapped areas, each with a sensitivity class (339 Moderate, 152 High, and 122 Less) and the area's size and perimeter. The CSV has no coordinates or shapes, so it can't be mapped or matched to Cuba on its own. Use for: a sensitivity indicator on the dashboard (Q9), once the map layer is downloaded and it's clear what "sensitivity" measures. Cautions: the class counts are numbers of mapped areas, not shares of land. The file doesn't state the units for area and perimeter.
docs.title: 3. Aquifer sensitivity

docs.text: Files: data4_monitoring-location-metadata.csv , data4_field-measurements.csv , data4_channel-measurements.csv Source: USGS station 08332525 on the Water Quality Portal The only dataset measured at Cuba itself: USGS station 08332525 on the Rio Puerco. The three files hold the station's details and coordinates, 4 gage-height readings (2019 to 2024), and 10 streamflow measurements (2019 to 2026). Six of the streamflow visits found no flow, and the other four measured 6.89 to 20.40 cubic feet per second. Use for: a scatter plot of flow by date, a count of zero-flow and flowing visits, and a map of the station relative to Cuba. Cautions: these are occasional visits, not a continuous record, so zero-flow readings don't mean the river is dry all year. The station measures the river, not Cuba's groundwater or water supply.
docs.title: 4. Rio Puerco at Cuba

docs.text: File: data5_ojo_alamo_sandstone_pub.pdf Source: USGS, Hydrogeology of the Ojo Alamo Sandstone in the San Juan Structural Basin (Hydrologic Atlas 720-B) A USGS map plate (1990) of the Ojo Alamo Sandstone across the San Juan Basin, showing depth to the top of the sandstone, its thickness, and wells completed in it. Use for: an annotated map, or a side-by-side comparison with the San Jose Formation (Q4). Cautions: this is a historical regional map, not current conditions, and it isn't a table to plot. It doesn't show that Cuba's wells draw from this formation.
docs.title: 5. Ojo Alamo Sandstone

docs.text: File: data6_cuba_mesa_member_of_san_jose_formation.pdf Source: Blandford et al. (2025), " San Jose Formation Hydrostratigraphy and Groundwater Conditions in the Vicinity of Lindrith, New Mexico ," New Mexico Geological Society Guidebook 75, pp. 235–246, doi:10.56577/FFC-75.235 A study of about 840 km² near Lindrith that uses more than 350 geophysical logs and 85 well-drilling logs. It identifies four water-bearing units in the San Jose Formation, maps the thickness of the Cuba Mesa Member, and maps groundwater levels. Use for: comparing with the Ojo Alamo Sandstone (Q4), and explaining which units wells reach (Q2). Cautions: the study is centered near Lindrith, not on Cuba's wells. The Cuba Mesa Member is a candidate water-bearing unit around Cuba, but the paper doesn't show that Cuba pumps from it.
docs.title: 6. San Jose Formation near Lindrith

Sections will cover groundwater levels, wells and aquifer units, the Cuba case study, water quality, acequias and surface water, and data gaps.
